title: One Honest Voice Against Four Hundred
overview: Two kings plan a war, a crowd of prophets promises victory, and one prophet who warns of disaster turns out to be right.

parts.label: An alliance and a war plan (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Jehoshaphat, king of the southern kingdom of Judah, tied his family to Ahab, king of the northern kingdom of Israel, by marrying his son to Ahab's daughter. Ahab then hosted a lavish feast and pressed him to help retake Ramoth Gilead, a town east of the Jordan River held by Aram (ancient Syria).

parts.label: Four hundred prophets say go (vv. 4-11)
parts.note: Jehoshaphat wanted to ask the LORD first, but Ahab's court prophets all promised victory, and Zedekiah acted it out with iron horns, a picture of a bull goring its enemies. Jehoshaphat seems uneasy with this chorus and asks whether there is another prophet.

parts.label: Micaiah's warning (vv. 12-17)
parts.note: Micaiah first repeats the crowd's answer, likely with sarcasm, since the king immediately demands the truth. His real message pictures Israel's army scattered like sheep with no shepherd, meaning the king will die and his soldiers will go home.

parts.label: A vision of heaven's court (vv. 18-22)
parts.note: Micaiah describes the LORD on a throne among heavenly beings, where a spirit offers to deceive Ahab through his own prophets so that he goes to his death. This is one of the Bible's most unsettling scenes, and interpreters disagree whether it shows God actively sending deception or is a vivid way of saying God let Ahab be fooled by the flattery he preferred.

parts.label: Slapped and jailed (vv. 23-27)
parts.note: Zedekiah strikes Micaiah, and Ahab sends him to prison on bread and water until the king returns safely. Micaiah stakes his whole credibility on the outcome: if Ahab comes back alive, the LORD did not speak through him.

parts.label: The battle and Ahab's death (vv. 28-34)
parts.note: Ahab disguises himself while Jehoshaphat, in royal robes, is nearly killed until he cries out and, as this book stresses, God turns the attackers away. A random arrow finds the gap in Ahab's armor, and he dies at sunset, just as Micaiah said.

disagreement: Christians genuinely differ on how to understand the deceiving spirit, whether God directly sent deception to bring judgment on Ahab or only permitted a deception Ahab had already chosen.
think: When nearly everyone around you agrees on something you want to hear, how do you tell whether they are right or just telling you what pleases you?
